extra.message: The application has no CSRF protection configured. Flask-WTF is installed but CSRFProtect is not initialized. None of the HTML forms include CSRF tokens, and no validation occurs on the server side.
The Flask app secret key is hardcoded as 'super secret key' in the source code. This key is used to sign session cookies and other security tokens.

The Flask secret key is set to a hardcoded, weak string 'super secret key'. This key is used to cryptographically sign session cookies. An attacker who knows the secret key can forge arbitrary session cookies, impersonate any user, including admin users.
The 404 error handler renders the error object's string representation and request.path into a template. The error object may contain verbose information about the server.

The 404 error handler passes `request.path` (user-controlled URL path) directly into a `render_template_string()` call via f-string. If the URL contains Jinja2 template syntax like `{{7*7}}` or `{{config}}`, it will be evaluated server-side. The `error` object's `__str__` output is also embedded.

The 404 error handler passes user-controlled request.path into render_template_string via an f-string. The resulting string is rendered as a Jinja2 template, enabling Server-Side Template Injection. An attacker can craft a URL path containing Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., {{config}}, {{''.__class__}}) which will be evaluated server-side, leading to RCE.

A static, hardcoded registration code 'a36e990b-0024-4d55-b74a-f8d7528e1764' is inserted into the database on every fresh setup. This code is the same across all installations and is publicly visible in the source code.

Default user accounts with hardcoded passwords ('user' for user@evfa.com and 'admin' for admin@evfa.com) are created in the database seed script. These passwords are embedded in source code, making them publicly known. Anyone can log in as 'user' or 'admin' using these passwords.

All forms use vanilla WTForms `Form` class instead of Flask-WTForms `FlaskForm`, which means no CSRF tokens are generated or validated. The application uses cookie-based sessions (Flask-Login), making CSRF attacks exploitable.

SQLAlchemy engine is configured with echo=True, which logs all SQL queries to stdout. In a production environment, this can expose sensitive data including user credentials, personal information, and database structure in logs.
The SQLAlchemy engine is configured with echo=True, which logs all SQL queries including potentially sensitive data (passwords, registration codes, etc.) to stdout.

The SQLAlchemy engine is configured with echo=True, which logs all SQL statements executed to stdout. This includes sensitive data from SQL queries such as passwords, registration codes, and note content.

The preferences cookie is set with `response.set_cookie()` without `httponly=True` or `secure=True` flags. Missing HttpOnly flag allows client-side JavaScript to access the cookie (though this cookie is non-sensitive). More importantly, the `after_request` handler also sets this cookie without httponly/secure. The app runs on port 5000 mapped to port 80 (HTTP).
The search endpoint (GET /search) has no rate limiting. Combined with the SQL injection vulnerability, this allows an attacker to perform automated data extraction via blind SQL injection.
The `search_param` from user-controlled query string is interpolated directly into a SQL text expression using an f-string. No parameterization or escaping is applied.

The `/accounts/<int:user_id>/notes` route accepts a user_id path parameter but never checks if the requesting user owns that user_id. Any authenticated user can view any other user's notes by changing the user_id.

The `/accounts/<user_id>/notes` route returns ALL notes for a given user_id with no access control check. Any authenticated user can view any other user's private notes by simply changing the user_id in the URL.
The get_personal_notes endpoint takes a user_id from the URL and returns all notes for that user without verifying that the requesting user owns those notes or has permission to view them.

The add_image endpoint (POST /account/image) has no rate limiting. Since this endpoint triggers an SSRF-prone URL fetch, unlimited access allows an attacker to perform extensive internal network scanning.
The profile image upload endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. An attacker can trick an authenticated victim into setting their profile image to a URL of the attacker's choosing.

User-controlled URL from the profile image form is passed to get_base64_image_blob() which downloads the URL with urllib.request.urlopen(). An attacker can provide a URL pointing to internal services.

The POST /account route (update_account function) is missing the @login_required decorator, allowing any unauthenticated user to modify account details. Combined with mass assignment, this allows anyone to escalate privileges.
The account update endpoint (POST /account) has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly change account details, perform mass password resets, or submit many update requests.

The `update_account()` route at `/account` (POST) is missing the `@login_required` decorator, unlike the GET route. Any authenticated or unauthenticated user can POST to this endpoint to modify account data.

The account update endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. An attacker can trick an authenticated victim into modifying account settings, including escalating privileges (exploiting the is_admin privilege escalation).

The `update_account()` handler updates `current_user.__dict__` with all non-None form fields except 'password'. The AccountForm includes an `is_admin` BooleanField, and there is no server-side check preventing non-admin users from setting `is_admin=true` in the POST body. The template only shows the is_admin checkbox for admin users, but there is no server-side validation. Any authenticated user can escalate to admin by sending `is_admin=true`.

The update_account handler updates current_user.__dict__ with all form values (except password). The AccountForm includes 'is_admin' which is not filtered, allowing a regular authenticated user to escalate to admin by POSTing is_admin=true.

The update_account handler applies all form fields (including 'is_admin') to the current user object via __dict__.update(). The AccountForm includes an is_admin BooleanField, allowing any authenticated user to escalate to admin by submitting is_admin=True.

The `filtered_values` from the form includes ALL non-None fields (except 'password'), including `is_admin`. This is applied directly to the user model via `current_user.__dict__.update(filtered_values)`. Any authenticated user can escalate themselves to admin by submitting `is_admin=1`.

The update_account handler allows changing the password without verifying the current/old password. The password_control field is a hidden field with the same value as the password field, not the current password.
The POST /darkmode route (toggle_darkmode function) is missing the @login_required decorator, allowing any unauthenticated user to access it.
The darkmode toggle endpoint (POST /darkmode) has no rate limiting. While low-impact, it's an unauthenticated state-changing endpoint that could be abused.
The dark mode toggle endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. Although lower impact, it demonstrates the systemic lack of CSRF protection.
The `preferences` cookie (and potentially session cookie) is set without `httponly`, `secure`, or `samesite` flags on the `set_cookie` calls.

The darkmode toggle serializes user preferences using pickle.dumps() before storing them in a cookie. While this is the write-side of the same issue, the vulnerability is the use of pickle for serializing untrusted data.

The before_request middleware reads the 'preferences' cookie from the client, base64-decodes it, and deserializes it using pickle.loads(). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution - an attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary Python code on the server.

User-controlled cookie `preferences` is base64-decoded and deserialized with `pickle.loads()` in the `before_request` handler. Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution.

Cookies are set without the `secure=True` flag, meaning the session cookie and preferences cookie can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, allowing session hijacking via network sniffing.
The login endpoint (POST /login) has no rate limiting, account lockout, failed attempt counter, CAPTCHA, or exponential backoff. This allows unlimited brute-force attacks against user passwords.

The do_login function does not regenerate the session ID after successful authentication. This allows session fixation attacks where an attacker can set a victim's session ID and then hijack the session after the victim logs in.

The login endpoint accepts POST requests without any CSRF protection. Since the application uses cookie-based sessions (Flask-Login), an attacker can craft a cross-site request that logs the victim into an attacker-controlled account, potentially revealing data in subsequent requests.

The login endpoint does not distinguish between 'user not found' and 'wrong password' cases - it always returns 'Invalid Credentials!'. However, the signup endpoint at routes/signup.py:58-59 explicitly reveals when a user already exists with 'User already exists', enabling user enumeration.
The do_login function calls login_user(user) without regenerating the session ID. This allows an attacker to potentially fixate a session ID and hijack the user's session after they log in.
The `/is_logged_in` endpoint returns the user's email without authentication, enabling username enumeration.
The /is_logged_in endpoint has no @login_required decorator, but this endpoint intentionally exposes authentication state. The issue is user enumeration via the username field.
The add_note endpoint (POST /notes) has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to mass-create notes and fill the database with spam or malicious content.
The note creation endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. An authenticated user's session could be used by an attacker to create notes on their behalf.
The delete_note function allows any authenticated user to delete any note by ID, without verifying that the note belongs to the current user. There is no ownership check before deleting.
The delete_note endpoint (POST /notes/<id>/delete) has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly delete many notes, combined with the IDOR vulnerability this enables mass data destruction.

The note deletion endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. An attacker can trick an authenticated victim into deleting notes, including notes belonging to other users (exploiting the IDOR vulnerability).

The delete_note endpoint fetches a note by ID and deletes it without verifying that the current user owns that note or is an admin. While the template conditionally shows the delete button only for note owners/admins, the server-side route has no such check, so any authenticated user can delete any note by directly POSTing to `/notes/<note_id>/delete`.
The registration code generation endpoint (POST /registration-codes) has no rate limiting, allowing an admin attacker or compromised admin account to generate unlimited registration codes.
The registration code generation endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. An admin's session could be used by an attacker to generate unlimited registration codes cross-site.
The `code` value from user registration form input is interpolated directly into a SQL query via f-string in `validate_token()`. No parameterization.
The signup endpoint (POST /signup) has no rate limiting. This allows an attacker to mass-register accounts, deplete the registration code pool, or perform enumeration attacks against existing users.
The signup endpoint accepts POST requests without CSRF protection. An attacker could trick a user into registering an account with credentials chosen by the attacker.

The registration code validation, verification, and deletion are not atomic. Between validate_token() checking the code exists and session.delete(token) removing it, a concurrent request with the same code could also pass validation and use the same code twice. With SQLite and multiple uwsgi workers, the race window exists.

The signup endpoint returns a different error message ('User already exists') when the email is already registered, compared to other error messages. This allows an attacker to enumerate registered user emails.

The profile image is rendered as a data URI in an <object> tag's data attribute. The image content is user-controlled (uploaded via URL). If an attacker uploads an SVG with embedded JavaScript as their profile image, it could execute when other users view it.

The profile image is rendered as a data URI in an <object> tag's data attribute in the navigation bar. The image content is user-controlled via URL upload. An attacker can upload a malicious SVG to execute JavaScript when other users view any page.

The note.text content is rendered with the |safe filter, which explicitly disables Jinja2's autoescaping. Since note.text is user-controlled (stored via the create note form and CKEditor), any user can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes when other users view notes on the home page.
Profile image rendered in note cards via <object> data URI with decoded profile_image.

The render_table function is called with safe_columns=['text'], which explicitly marks the 'text' column as safe HTML. Since note.text is user-controlled (stored via the create note form), any user can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes when another user views the personal notes page.

The client-side CSV export function in personal_notes.html does not sanitize cells that start with spreadsheet formula characters (`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`). When the CSV is opened in Excel, LibreOffice, or Google Sheets, formula injection can execute arbitrary commands or exfiltrate data.

The render_table function is called with safe_columns=['text'], which explicitly marks the 'text' column as safe HTML. Since note.text is user-controlled and stored in the database, this enables stored XSS when users view search results.
The download() function uses urlopen() without a timeout. An attacker can provide a URL that connects but never sends a response (slow loris), holding the server worker indefinitely.
The download() function calls urlopen() directly on a user-controlled URL without any validation, redirect following, or timeout. This is the SSRF sink.
